headlines.title: Cruise companies aim to keep fuel costs down. Their strategies for doing so differ
headlines.summary: Carnival is cutting fuel use, while Royal Caribbean and Norwegian rely on "hedging" to keep fuel costs down amid conflict in the Middle East.
headlines.article_text: How Carnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian keep fuel costs down Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Carnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian reported strong third-quarter earnings despite rising fuel prices. Executives from Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Cruise Line maintain that "hedging" will help protect them from rising costs, while Carnival's CEO says cutting fuel consumption works best. All three cruise companies expect fuel costs or consumption to continue to rise in the fourth quarter. In this article CCL RCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Docked and arriving cruise ships in Cozumel, Mexico. Jeff Greenberg | Universal Images Group | Getty Images Carnival , Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings posted strong earnings for their most recent quarters despite rising fuel prices. How the leading cruise companies navigate fuel costs boils down to starkly different strategies. Oil prices have skyrocketed since the U.S.-Israel war with Iran began on Feb. 28. Brent crude oil reached a six-month high on Friday, settling at $116.72 per barrel. With no clear end in sight for the conflict in the Middle East, the pressure affecting cruise ships' lifeblood seems poised to last into the holiday travel season and beyond. Both Royal Caribbean and Norwegian practice "hedging," or a strategy of using derivatives to reduce exposure to future fuel-price swings, to account for sharp price changes. Carnival CEO Josh Weinstein, on the other hand, told CNBC in an interview last month that cutting fuel consumption is the best way to avert the effects of expensive fuel. "At the end of the day, fuel is an input cost for us. The best thing that we can do to control that cost is to use less," Weinstein said at the time. Jefferies analyst David Katz told CNBC in an interview that companies that hedge do so primarily to manage the cost of fuel, but also to manage Wall Street expectations and prevent hectic stock trading based on fuel price fluctuations. "When you're public, the Street will trade your stock around based on the price of fuel," Katz said. "The Street's argument is that volatility puts pressure on your multiple." "While it is mathematically most likely true that over the long term it is more expensive," he explained. "The benefit of having less fuel volatility in the model and less trading volatility is [it's] good for your multiple." Despite the potential positives of the strategy, Carnival has maintained the stance it has held since 2019: Cutting fuel consumption works better than hedging. And Carnival's third-quarter earnings report last month suggests the strategy may be paying off. Carnival's 'maniacal' cutting Carnival beat analysts' expectations on both the top and bottom lines for its most recent quarter and reported an all-time high net income of $1.9 billion. VIDEO 6:24 06:24 Watch CNBC's full interview with Carnival CEO Josh Weinstein Weinstein told CNBC in an interview on "Squawk on the Street" following the release that the company has been "maniacal" about cutting its fuel consumption, saying it's slashed its unit fuel consumption rate by 26% since 2019. "We estimate we've saved about $700 million in 2026 based on that consumption savings rate going down since 2019," he said. Carnival spent $615 million, or about 7.3% of its revenue, on fuel in the third quarter, according to its most recent earnings release. That's an increase from the $425 million, or 6.7% of revenue, that the company spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, before fuel prices spiked. Carnival projects its fuel costs will rise to $640 million in the fourth quarter, according to its earnings release. Careful hedging VIDEO 6:36 06:36 Watch CNBC's full interview with Royal Caribbean CEO Jason Liberty Royal Caribbean similarly beat analyst expectations for earnings per share for its third quarter, reported Tuesday. However, it narrowly missed on revenue. CEO Jason Liberty attributed the company's beat in part to its hedging strategy during an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Tuesday morning. "We're a little bit over 60% hedged here for 2026, and so that's helping insulate us from some of the impacts on the rising fuel costs," he said. "It's obviously still impacting us," Liberty said. "[High fuel prices] evaporated a good chunk of our Q3 earnings beat into the full-year guide. But we're continuing to hedge, and we watch." Royal Caribbean spent about $347 million on fuel in the third quarter, or about 6.2% of its revenue, according to its earnings release. That compares with $293 million, or 6.8% of revenue, spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, which ended on Dec. 31. The company projects fuel costs will continue to rise to $379 million in the fourth quarter. Liberty pointed out that high fuel prices have not dampened demand from consumers for vacations. "It's not that we don't see points of challenges, but really what we've seen is that even in those points of challenges, the consumer comes roaring back," he said. Royal Caribbean reported strong bookings for the third quarter and said reservations for 2027 are already up by a high-teens percentage. Norwegian's continued bet Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings beat on both the top and bottom lines for its third-quarter earnings, reported on Thursday, with revenue of $2.9 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $1.12. The company has hedged approximately 48% of its fuel consumption for 2026, according to the earnings release. Norwegian spent about $196 million on fuel in the third quarter, or about 6.6% of its revenue, according to its most recent earnings release. That's a lower share of revenue than the 7.4% — totaling $167 million — spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, which ended on Dec. 31. The company projects fuel consumption to rise slightly in the fourth quarter, up to 255,000 metric tons from 239,000 metric tons consumed in the third quarter. The company is in the midst of a turnaround effort. And despite facing added challenges from the macro environment, CFO Mark Kempa said he is reassured by this quarter's results on an earnings call on Thursday. "These results reinforce our confidence in the appeal of our products and the opportunity to translate stronger revenue performance and disciplined cost management into improved profitability," Kempa said. headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: ADT, Alphabet, Caterpillar, Eli Lilly, Chipotle & more
headlines.summary: These are the stocks posting the largest moves midday.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: ADT, GOOGL, CAT, LLY, CMG Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves midday: ADT — The home security stock soared about 34% after ADT said it will be acquired by Thrive Holdings in an all-cash $15.3 billion transaction. The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. Glaukos — The pharma company focused on ophthalmic diseases saw shares surge 32% after it reported third-quarter results. Glaukos posted revenue of $211 million, topping a FactSet consensus of $168 million. Adjusted earnings per share came in at 47 cents, though it wasn't clear if that was comparable with estimates. The company also raised its full-year revenue guidance. Textron — The aircraft and defense systems manufacturer's stock rallied nearly 15% on third-quarter earnings that beat expectations. Textron earned $1.76 per share, excluding certain items, exceeding a FactSet estimate of $1.43 per share. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook. Boot Barn — Shares of the apparel retailer jumped almost 14%. Second-quarter gross margin beat expectations, landing at 37.2% versus the StreetAccount consensus estimate of 36.6%. Second-quarter earnings of $1.73 per share on revenue of $581.8 million beat analysts' call for $1.64 per share and $580.8 million, per FactSet. Sprouts Farmers Market — The grocery store chain's stock tumbled 22% on third-quarter earnings and revenue that came in below expectations. The company also slashed its full-year earnings per share outlook to around $4.80 from a previous range of $5.32 to $5.40 per share. Alphabet — Shares dropped close to 12% after the Google parent's third-quarter earnings showed the company posted negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion. Its core search revenue of $63.35 billion missed the $64.96 billion estimate from analysts. Total company revenue of $127.58 billion also missed LSEG expectations of $128.22 billion. Caterpillar — Shares slid more than 7% even after the company reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that beat the Street. The company earned an adjusted $7.20 per share on revenue of $20.68 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG expected a profit of $7.08 per share on revenue of $20.55 billion. However, sales for its construction industries business came in slightly below estimates. DoorDash , Maplebear — DoorDash announced it is acquiring the Instacart parent for $65 per share. That is an 11% premium from Maplebear's closing price on Wednesday. DoorDash also reported a revenue and EBITDA beat for its third quarter. Maplebear's stock was down almost 2%, while shares of DoorDash rose 4%. Eli Lilly — The Zepbound and Mounjaro maker handily beat expectations for its third quarter, sending shares 6% higher. Eli Lilly saw adjusted earnings of $7.48 per share, compared with the consensus estimate $6.26 a share, per LSEG. Revenue came in at $24.4 billion, topping the $22.61 billion expected from analysts. Marvell Technology , Lumentum — Lumentum shares gained 3% after Bloomberg News reported, citing sources that the data center optics manufacturer was in talks to be acquired by Marvell. A deal could be announced as soon as next week, the report said . Marvell shares dropped more than 11%. Shell — Shares climbed 2% after the oil major nearly doubled its third-quarter profit from the year prior to $10.81 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG were expecting $9.92 billion. Norwegian Cruise Line — The cruise operator jumped 13% following its beat on the top and bottom lines. Norwegian reported adjusted earnings of $1.12 per share, topping the consensus estimate of 93 cents, according to FactSet. Revenue was $2.95 billion, versus the $2.88 billion anticipated by analysts. Chipotle Mexican Grill — Shares gained 8% after the burrito chain reported same-store sales that beat estimates. Same-store sales in the third quarter grew 2.1%, versus the 1.5% increase analysts polled by FactSet anticipated. ServiceNow — The enterprise software company's shares tumbled 26%. Third-quarter adjusted profit of $1 per share missed the LSEG consensus expectation of $1.02 a share. Subscription revenue guidance for the fourth quarter ranged from $4.245 billion to $4.255 billion, while the FactSet consensus called for $4.25 billion. Fortinet — The cybersecurity company's stock plummeted 21%. Non-GAAP gross margin for the third quarter came in at 79.6%, while analysts polled by LSEG sought 80.1%. Separately, top- and bottom-line results beat the Street's expectations. Crocs — The footwear stock surged nearly 26% after Crocs posted third-quarter earnings that beat expectations, and it issued stronger-than-expected current-quarter guidance. It posted earnings of $3.69 per share, excluding items, on revenue of $1.04 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet anticipated earnings of $3.31 per share on revenue of $1 billion. eBay — Shares climbed more than 3% after the company reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter results. Revenue rose 14% to $3.2 billion, while gross merchandise volume increased 15%. Growth from Depop, accelerating GMV, and raised full-year guidance gave investors further confidence in eBay's strategy. Honeywell Aerospace — Shares were down 10% even after the aerospace company raised its full-year outlook for pro forma standalone adjusted earnings per share, calling for $7.85 to $8. The company also announced an initial quarterly cash dividend of 40 cents per share. Carvana — The used car dealer's stock climbed 15%. Carvana third-quarter revenue and adjusted EBITDA topped the numbers Wall Street had been expecting, and it said the Securities and Exchange Commission closed a previously disclosed investigation and would not take any enforcement action. — CNBC's Darla Mercado, Sarah Min, Paulina Likos, Scott Schnipper, Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells contributed reporting.

headlines.article_text: Eli Lilly (LLY) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Eli Lilly reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past estimates and hiked its full-year sales outlook. Demand for its obesity drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro surged again and topped estimates for the quarter. In this article LLY Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:53 04:53 Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks on the obesity market: The room for expansion is dramatic Squawk on the Street Eli Lilly on Thursday reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past estimates and hiked its full-year sales outlook, as demand for its blockbuster weight loss drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro soared again. Despite that strength, sales of its new GLP-1 obesity pill Foundayo, which launched in the U.S. in April, were under Wall Street's expectations for the quarter. The pharmaceutical giant now expects 2026 revenue to come in between $91 billion and $92 billion, up from a previous guidance of $85 billion to $87 billion. Lilly projects its full-year adjusted earnings will be between $35 and $36 per share, which compares with a previous outlook of $35.50 to $36.50 per share. The company said it raised the underlying profit guidance by $4.07 per share at the midpoint, but noted that it is offset by $4.57 per share in charges tied to deals in the quarter. The company's shares rose about 7% on Thursday. Lilly's massive diabetes and obesity windfall – and market share lead over chief rival Novo – shows no signs of slowing down, even as the company grapples with lower net prices in the U.S. The pharma giant is converting its massive profits into a deal-making spree, most recently striking an agreement to buy Merida Biosciences to develop a new class of treatments for serious autoimmune and allergic diseases. Here's what Eli Lilly reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $7.48 adjusted vs. $6.26 expected Revenue: $24.40 billion vs. $22.61 billion expected Resilient demand for Zepbound and Mounjaro has helped fuel several strong quarters for Lilly despite lower prices for the medications in the U.S., which came after a drug pricing deal struck with the Trump administration last year. In a release, Lilly also pointed to expanded U.S. coverage for obesity care, referring to Medicare's decision to start covering GLP-1s for weight loss in July under a temporary pilot program. "This is a program that's really working," Lilly CEO Dave Ricks said on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ." "We're pleased with the early uptake and access, and I think doctors and patients are as well." Mounjaro's worldwide revenue rose 65% to $10.72 billion for the quarter, including U.S. sales of about $5 billion. That surpassed the $10.10 billion in worldwide sales and $4.79 billion in U.S. revenue that analysts were expecting for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Mounjaro notably saw strength internationally, with sales outside the U.S. jumping 93%. Zepbound, which entered the market roughly three years ago, posted $5.35 billion in revenue for the third quarter. That's up 49% from the year-earlier period, as demand for the drug also rose while realized prices dropped. The vast majority of those sales came from the U.S. Analysts were expecting $5.09 billion in global sales for Zepbound, including $4.99 billion from the U.S., according to StreetAccount. The Eli Lilly logo appears on the company’s office in San Diego, California, Nov. 21, 2025. Mike Blake | Reuters Lilly's newly launched obesity pill, Foundayo, which won U.S. approval in April, took in $184 million in sales for the third quarter. That fell under analyst forecasts of around $229 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates showed. It marks the second earnings report that includes revenue from the GLP-1 pill, which is competing head-to-head with a rival oral drug from Novo that launched in January. Total U.S. prescriptions for Foundayo and the number of new Foundayo patients in the third quarter doubled from the previous quarter, Lilly CFO Lucas Montarces said during a Thursday earnings call. Around 4 in 10 patients starting an oral obesity medicine choose Foundayo, he added. Lilly expects Foundayo to win U.S. approval for Type 2 diabetes in the fourth quarter. Lilly is working to maintain its dominance in the booming market for GLP-1 drugs, with the company holding 63% share of the U.S. obesity and diabetes drug market in the third quarter, according to an earnings presentation on Thursday. Novo's market share in the quarter was 36.6%. During the earnings call, Montarces said 7 out of 10 U.S. prescriptions for injectable obesity and diabetes drugs in the third quarter were for a Lilly medicine. Ricks told CNBC that he estimates 3% to 10% of eligible patients access obesity care in the U.S., but said the "room for expansion here of this market is dramatic." Lilly is at the front of that push, he added. Internationally, Lilly held 58.4% share of the market, while Novo had 41.6%, the presentation said. Eli Lilly's revenue in the U.S. climbed 34% to $15.1 billion. Lilly said it saw a 41% increase in volume — or the number of prescriptions or units sold — for its products, primarily for Mounjaro and Zepbound. That was partially offset by a 7% decrease in realized prices, primarily driven by Zepbound. Lilly's quarter was also boosted by a sales-based milestone payout of $410 million for its Type 2 diabetes medication Jardiance, related to the company's collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim. Sales outside the U.S. jumped 47% to $9.3 billion, propelled by a 76% surge in volume and partly offset by a 29% drop in realized prices. The pharmaceutical giant booked net income of $6.45 billion, or $7.22 per share, for the third quarter, which includes the $4.57 per share deal charges. That compares with net income of $5.58 billion, or $6.21 per share, a year earlier. Excluding one-time items associated with the value of intangible assets and other adjustments, Eli Lilly posted earnings of $7.48 per share for the third quarter. headlines.article_text: Alphabet earnings miss first sign AI is taking a bite out of search Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Wall Street hammered Alphabet for an earnings miss that included weaker-than-expected revenue in the company's core business. Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. Regarding new AI agents and bots, Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said, "These things are going to be a force." In this article GOOGL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:44 06:44 Alphabet misses Wall Street expectation on earnings, stock continues to slide in extended trading Fast Money In Alphabet's across-the-board earnings miss , one segment stood out above all else: search. Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. At the same time, Google said search query growth on the platform was the strongest it's been in five years. The gap between usage and revenue within the search giant's flagship business is becoming harder to dismiss as more people turn to artificial intelligence bots and agents, including tools offered by Google. Since the early days of ChatGPT, analysts have predicted that traditional search will get eclipsed by AI, and warned that Google will have to figure out new ways to make money. While search remains a massive business, early signs of a shift are appearing. "These things are going to be a force," Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster told CNBC's " Fast Money " after the earnings report, referring to new AI-powered services. Munster said that if "personalized bots" take off, "that will become for a lot of people the starting point of commerce, which impacts where Google is." watch now VIDEO 5:16 05:16 AI search queries hurt Alphabet's core business, says Deepwater's Gene Munster Fast Money Alphabet executives said foreign exchange was the biggest factor behind the deceleration in search revenue in the period, and said the currency impact would be even greater in the fourth quarter. The stock plummeted about 10% in extended trading, reflecting the weaker-than-expected earnings report and negative free cash flow of $9 billion for the quarter, three times the estimated deficit. In the second quarter, Alphabet's free cash flow went negative for the first time in its history as a public company, at $5.9 billion. Google has spent much of the past year telling investors that it needs to pour money into AI infrastructure and services to meet unending demand from consumers and businesses. Google's Gemini model has allowed the company to stay competitive with Anthropic and OpenAI , and its Gemini-powered enterprise services have proven to be a hit with customers. The company also says that Gemini is strengthening its core digital ads business, as it uses AI to improve its ability to understand user intent and make advertising more relevant. “We continue to accelerate the deployment of Gemini models across our entire ads infrastructure to boost performance,” Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said on the third-quarter earnings call. Advertisers are also rapidly adopting AI tools. In the third quarter, Gemini models helped advertisers generate more than 1.5 billion campaign assets, up more than sevenfold from a year earlier, Schindler said. watch now VIDEO 3:04 03:04 Google's AI spending surges: Here's what you need to know Squawk on the Street But none of that addresses revenue growth for search, which slid from 19% in the first quarter to 17% in the second, before falling to 12% in the third. Analysts at UBS wrote in a note that the results are "going to bring Search cannibalization fears right back to the forefront." And Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein said the numbers are an issue for search and YouTube. "This elevates the fear around AI and agentic taking share from Search and YT and hurting their AI monetization narrative," Klein wrote in a note after the earnings report. Cloud gives Alphabet its AI payoff Where Alphabet's AI bet is very much paying off is in its cloud business. Revenue in that division, which is racing to catch up to Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, more than doubled in the quarter to nearly $31 billion. Cloud backlog also reached roughly $560 billion, reflecting enormous contracted demand for AI infrastructure. Management said it expects just more than half of that backlog to be recognized over the next 24 months. In Microsoft's quarterly earnings report , which also landed after the bell Wednesday, the software maker said Azure revenue increased 48% from a year earlier to $33.2 billion. Cloud demand is a big reason for Alphabet to keep spending. The company maintained its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending will increase significantly in 2027. Some of that is for its tensor processing units , or TPUs, which compete with Nvidia's graphics processing units. Alphabet just started selling them to outside customers in the second quarter. Google released its 7th generation TPU, Ironwood, in November 2025, a decade after making its first custom ASIC for AI in 2015. Denis Balibouse | Ruben Sprich | Reuters The past few quarters of hyperscaler earnings have been marked by ever-increasing capital expenditure forecasts as tech giants race to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure to meet what they describe as insatiable demand. At least for the moment, Microsoft and Alphabet are telling a slightly different story. In their earnings reports Wednesday, both companies shared capex figures that came up shy of analysts' estimates. Microsoft reduced its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, and Alphabet held its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion. The numbers suggest a slowdown is nowhere in sight, but they do represent another potential point of concern for the AI buildout. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN all dropped after the reports, as did Oracle , which is one of the biggest spenders on AI infrastructure. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on the software company's earnings call that third-party providers of graphics processing units had delays that will push out some available capacity until the first half of 2027. She didn't provide names, but Microsoft relies on CoreWeave, IREN and Nebius, among others. Anat Ashkenazi , Alphabet's finance chief, told analysts that outside computing power "came online only at the very end of Q3." Alphabet shares tumbled about 10% in extended trading as the company missed on earnings and revenue and reported negative free cash flow of more than $9 billion. Plenty of Alphabet shareholders remain faithful. "We are pleased with what we see and what we heard, and trust management's approach to their AI spending," Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, wrote in an email to CNBC. Investors will get a final read on hyperscaler capex for the quarter when Amazon reports results after the close Thursday. In Meta's earnings report last week, the company said it expects full-year capex of $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. Like with Alphabet, Meta shares sank as the company reported negative free cash flow. watch now VIDEO 4:33 04:33 Free cashflow or AI capex? Markets don't know what they want, says Albion's Ware Squawk Box Asia Delays from emerging neocloud partners have occurred before at Microsoft, but they're more critical now as Anthropic gets set to go public. Anthropic counts on infrastructure from Amazon, Google and Microsoft for much of its computing needs, alongside capacity from SpaceX , Lambda and Nscale, which filed to go public in September but hasn't updated its prospectus in weeks. At times this year, Anthropic's Claude assistant has been unavailable due to climbing demand. Rival OpenAI , which has said an initial public offering in 2027 is likely, is also in constant need of more capacity. One big challenge for the market is that the neoclouds require billions of dollars in outside capital to fuel their buildouts but don't have investment-grade credit ratings. With interest rates rising and concerns about their debt loads mounting, lenders are pulling out of the market. Last week, analysts at Gartner shared with CNBC the firm's prediction that, by 2030, 80% of neocloud companies will either be absorbed or completely cease operations. Nvidia -backed neocloud Firmus, based in Australia, withdrew plans to go public earlier this month, despite boasting large usage commitments from Meta and OpenAI. None of that is to suggest the AI buildout is over, or even close to plateauing. Microsoft's Hood said Wednesday that she sees capital spending accelerating in the first half of 2027 thanks to higher component costs and the delayed deliveries. As a group, hyperscaler capex is expected to top $1 trillion next year and, according to some estimates , continue rising from there. Despite the third-quarter capex shortfall, investors cheered Microsoft's report on Wednesday as the company beat earnings and revenue estimates, driven by 48% sales growth in its Azure cloud business. "We view the quarter as further validation of Microsoft's AI-led growth opportunity," Cantor analysts led by Thomas Blakey wrote in a Wednesday note to clients. They recommend buying Microsoft stock, and they pushed up their one-year price target to $630 from $608. headlines.title: Beyond the Ticker: Why Companies Are Choosing Nasdaq
headlines.summary: A generation ago, the choice of where to list was closely tied to where a company’s peers and sector traded. But as U.S. market structure evolved, that relationship fundamentally changed. Today, a company’s shares can trade across multiple venues throughout the day, with orders routed across the market in search of the best available price, regardless of where the stock is listed. That evolution has changed the question companies should ask when choosing a listing venue. It is no longer simply, “Where should our stock trade?” Increasingly, it is, “Who do we want as our partner in the public markets?” The answer matters. A listing venue should deliver more than a place for a ticker. It should help a company succeed as a public company through market quality and liquidity, technology, investor intelligence, visibility, advocacy and support throughout its public-company journey.

headlines.title: Amazon to report Q3 earnings after the bell with AI spend under scrutiny
headlines.summary: Amazon Web Services sales are projected to grow 38%, marking a fifth consecutive quarter of revenue expansion.
headlines.article_text: Amazon (AMZN) Q3 earnings report 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Wall Street is paying close attention to Amazon's cloud growth and artificial intelligence spending. Amazon Web Services sales are projected to grow 38%, marking a fifth consecutive quarter of revenue expansion. The company will hold a conference call with investors to discuss the results at 5:00 p.m. ET. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Andy Jassy, CEO of Amazon, speaks during an unveiling event in New York, Feb. 26, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Amazon is slated to report third-quarter earnings results after the bell on Thursday. Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.96 adjusted Revenue: $202.31 billion Wall Street is also looking at other key revenue numbers: Amazon Web Services: $45.48 billion, according to StreetAccount Advertising: $20.82 billion, according to StreetAccount Investors expect to see robust growth in Amazon's cloud segment. AWS sales are predicted to grow 38%, according to StreetAccount, compared with a 37% gain last quarter. It would mark AWS's fifth consecutive quarter of revenue acceleration. That momentum isn't expected to slow down. CEO Andy Jassy said Amazon's cloud capacity is "largely sold out" for next year, and it's received significant commitments for 2028 as well. "We always leave a certain amount for on demand and our inference service Bedrock or EC2, but largely sold out all the big chunks," Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week. "A good chunk of '28 is sold out." Wall Street will be listening for any commentary from Amazon executives around AI spending. Last quarter, the company hiked its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 to $220 billion, up from $200 billion. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount expect Amazon's capex to creep up more than $280 billion in 2027. Read more CNBC tech news AI build-out hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecasts Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search As Waymo expands overseas, it remains a niche cash-burning business Hands-on with Apple’s first touchscreen laptop: Touch is totally optional Amazon has rushed to bring more data centers online to meet surging demand for AI computing power. The aggressive spending has eaten into the company's cash flow . In July, the company reported negative free cash flow of $7.6 billion for the trailing twelve months, compared with positive free cash flow of $18.2 billion one year earlier. It's expected to be cash flow negative in the current quarter, with an outflow of $9.9 billion, according to FactSet estimates. Alphabet and Meta both reported negative free cash flow in their latest quarterly earnings reports. Microsoft said Wednesday its free cash flow declined 27% in the fiscal first quarter, but its cash flow remained positive, unlike its hyperscaler peers. As Amazon shells out more on AI, it's steadily trimmed its headcount. The company has laid off more than 57,000 staffers since 2022, or roughly 16% of its corporate workforce. The job cuts have continued on a rolling basis this year via smaller rounds of layoffs. The company on Wednesday laid off some staffers in its device software and services team to "operate more efficiently and better align with our product roadsmap," an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to CNBC. Fewer than 250 employees were let go as a result of the job cuts, the company said. During the third quarter, Amazon made headlines when it blocked Meta 's Muse AI agent from shopping on its platform. The company said it was not given advance notice that Muse would access its webstore, and it never agreed to participate. The move is in line with Amazon's broader stance on third-party agents accessing its site. Amazon has blocked dozens of external agents, including Perplexity , which the company sued last year over allegations that the startup concealed its AI shopping bots. Amazon stock chart. While it locks down its site from third-party agents, Amazon has increasingly invested in its own tools. In May, Amazon rebranded its Rufus AI shopping chatbot to Alexa for Shopping. On Thursday, Amazon said more than 400 million shoppers have used the assistant, and the number of people using Alexa for Shopping's agentic features has "grown more than eight times since the start of the year." The tool now has more than 100 shopping-related capabilities, the company said, including the ability to build gift lists, manage subscriptions and handle account changes. As rivals Meta and OpenAI push deeper into AI shopping tools, analysts have said the services could pose a risk to Amazon's digital advertising business. Users are turning to services like Muse and ChatGPT to research products, or in some cases, handing off purchases to AI agents, which means they're bypassing sponsored ads on Amazon's site. "We expect Amazon to eventually develop its own agentic shopping offering, with its proprietary purchase data and commerce infrastructure positioning it well," Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note last week.
